counterexample:
Take the diamond lattice M3: S = {0, a, b, c, 1} ordered by 0 < a < 1, 0 < b < 1, 0 < c < 1, with a, b, c pairwise incomparable.

(i) M3 is a lattice: every pair has a join and a meet. For distinct x, y in {a,b,c}: x \/ y = 1 and x /\ y = 0; 0 is the bottom and 1 the top, so 0 /\ x = 0, 0 \/ x = x, 1 /\ x = x, 1 \/ x = 1.

(ii) M3 is a COMPLETE lattice: it is finite with a bottom 0 and a top 1, so every subset T of S has a supremum and an infimum (sup of the empty set = 0, inf of the empty set = 1, and finite non-empty sups/infs exist by (i) and associativity). Hence M3 is an object of CLat.

(iii) M3 is NOT a frame: take the element a and the subset T = {b, c}. Then
    a /\ \/T = a /\ (b \/ c) = a /\ 1 = a,
while
    \/{a /\ t : t in T} = (a /\ b) \/ (a /\ c) = 0 \/ 0 = 0.
Since a != 0, the (infinite) distributive law a /\ \/T = \/{a /\ t} fails, so M3 is not a frame and is NOT an object of Frm.

Therefore the objects of CLat are not a subcollection of the objects of Frm, contradicting step 0002. The same witness also kills the morphism half of step 0002: the identity mapping id_{M3} : M3 -> M3 preserves all suprema and infima, so it is a complete lattice homomorphism and hence a morphism of CLat; but it is not a morphism of Frm at all, since Frm contains no morphism with domain or codomain M3 (M3 is not an object of Frm). Consequently CLat is not a subcategory of Frm, so the theorem statement as well as step 0002 is false.

(Note: the cited result 'Complete Lattice Homomorphism is Frame Homomorphism' only compares morphism classes between lattices that are already frames; it gives no ground for the object-inclusion claim in step 0002.)
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0002 are the first substantive claim and they fail. The citation (Complete Lattice Homomorphism is Frame Homomorphism) speaks only about morphisms; it provides no justification for the assertion that the objects of CLat form a subcollection of the objects of Frm. That object-inclusion claim is in fact false: an object of Frm is a complete lattice satisfying the infinite distributive law, whereas an object of CLat is an arbitrary complete lattice, and complete lattices need not be distributive. The diamond M3 is a finite (hence complete) lattice with a /\ (b \/ c) = a but (a /\ b) \/ (a /\ c) = 0, so it lies in CLat but not in Frm; likewise id_{M3} is a CLat morphism that is not a Frm morphism. Since a subcategory must have a subcollection of objects (and of morphisms), step 0002 is wrong and the concluding step 0009 inherits the error. Steps 0004-0007 (composition is composition of mappings, identities are identity mappings in both categories) are correct in themselves but cannot repair the object-inclusion failure. Verification stopped at step 0002 with the witness above.
